hints: Think about how diamond and graphite are built up, a continuous network of carbon atoms joined by strong covalent bonds extending throughout the crystal, not separate small molecules.
walkthrough:
Picture what holds the crystal together**
Imagine diamond and graphite at the atomic level. You do not have separate $\text{C}_2$ or $\text{C}_6$ molecules sitting next to each other. You have millions of carbon atoms all covalently bonded into one continuous 3D network in diamond, or into continuous layers in graphite. That continuous covalent network is the definition of giant molecular.
Final answer: Both have a giant molecular (giant covalent) lattice structure.

hints: Recall how many bonds each carbon forms in graphite and what happens to the fourth outer electron that is not used in sigma bonding.
walkthrough:
Count the bonding in graphite**
Each carbon in graphite bonds to only three other carbons in its layer. Carbon has four outer electrons, so three are used in covalent sigma bonds and the fourth is left over on every carbon.

Link mobile electrons to conduction**
Those leftover p electrons overlap sideways to form a delocalised system above and below each layer. Because they are no longer fixed to one atom, they can move through the layers when a voltage is applied, and moving charged particles is exactly what an electric current is.
Final answer: Graphite has delocalised electrons that can move through the structure / between the layers to carry charge.

hints: Compare with graphite by counting how many other carbons each carbon is bonded to in diamond and whether any outer electron is left free to move.
walkthrough:
See why diamond is different**
In diamond every carbon is tetrahedrally bonded to four other carbons. All four outer electrons are locked into four strong localised sigma bonds. There is no spare electron to become delocalised.

Conclude about conductivity**
For a solid to conduct, it needs mobile charged particles. With no ions free to move and no delocalised electrons, diamond has no charge carrier, so it cannot conduct even though it is also giant molecular.
Final answer: Diamond has no delocalised electrons to carry charge, as all 4 outer electrons of each carbon are used in covalent bonding.

hints: Remember that both $\text{PCl}_5$ and $\text{SiCl}_4$ are fully hydrolysed by water to give $\text{HCl}$ plus the corresponding acid or oxide.
Balance atoms by thinking of $\text{PCl}_5$ giving phosphoric acid $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$ and $\text{SiCl}_4$ giving solid silicon dioxide $\text{SiO}_2$.
walkthrough:
Recognise complete hydrolysis**
Period 3 chlorides from $\text{Al}$ to $\text{P}$ react vigorously with water. $\text{PCl}_5$ and $\text{SiCl}_4$ are not just dissolved, they react to replace every $\text{Cl}$ with $\text{O}$ or $\text{OH}$, releasing $\text{HCl}$ gas which dissolves to give an acidic solution.

Write the phosphorus equation**
Phosphorus(V) ends up as phosphoric acid: $$\text{PCl}_5 + 4\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{H}_3\text{PO}_4 + 5\text{HCl}$$ Check: 5 $\text{Cl}$ need 5 $\text{HCl}$, so you need 4 $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to supply 8 $\text{H}$ and 4 $\text{O}$.

Write the silicon equation**
Silicon(IV) ends up as silicon dioxide, which is insoluble: $$\text{SiCl}_4 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{SiO}_2 + 4\text{HCl}$$ Check: 4 $\text{Cl}$ need 4 $\text{HCl}$, so 2 $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ supplies the 4 $\text{H}$ and 2 $\text{O}$ needed.

Final answer: $\text{PCl}_5 + 4\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{H}_3\text{PO}_4 + 5\text{HCl}$
$\text{SiCl}_4 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{SiO}_2 + 4\text{HCl}$

hints: Recall the trend in Period 3 chlorides from solid $\text{AlCl}_3$ and $\text{PCl}_5$ to volatile liquids, which one is a fuming liquid at room temperature.
Think of the typical bottle labels, $\text{PCl}_5$ as a pale solid that fumes in air and $\text{SiCl}_4$ as a volatile colourless liquid.
walkthrough:
Fix the starting appearances**
Before water is added, you must describe the reagents themselves. $\text{PCl}_5$ is an ionic-like solid at room temperature, seen as a white to pale yellow solid. $\text{SiCl}_4$ is a simple molecular liquid, seen as a colourless fuming liquid.

Avoid confusing with products**
Do not describe steamy fumes or solutions here. That comes in the next part. This part is only the appearance of the pure chlorides in their bottles at room temperature.

Final answer: phosphorus(V) chloride: white / yellow solid
silicon(IV) chloride: colourless liquid

hints: Use your equations from (b)(i) to decide which non-HCl product is fully soluble in water and which is an insoluble oxide.
Remember that $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$ gives a clear homogeneous solution while $\text{SiO}_2$ forms a fine white solid dispersed in liquid.
walkthrough:
Follow the products into water**
From (b)(i), $\text{PCl}_5$ hydrolysis gives $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$ plus $\text{HCl}$. Both are very soluble, so the solid disappears completely to leave a homogeneous colourless acidic solution.

Spot the insoluble product**
$\text{SiCl}_4$ hydrolysis gives $\text{SiO}_2$ plus $\text{HCl}$. $\text{SiO}_2$ is a giant covalent solid and is insoluble, so you see a white suspension or white precipitate dispersed in the colourless acidic liquid. The contrast, solution versus suspension, is the comparison needed.

Final answer: phosphorus(V) chloride mixture: colourless solution
silicon(IV) chloride mixture: white suspension / white precipitate in a colourless liquid / mixture / solution

hints: Think of the word ampho meaning both, what two opposite types of reagent can this oxide react with.
walkthrough:
Unpack the term simply**
Amphoteric means dual behaviour. An amphoteric oxide can neutralise an acid acting as a base, and can also neutralise a base acting as an acid. It reacts in both directions, unlike basic oxides which react only with acids and acidic oxides which react only with bases.
Final answer: An amphoteric species behaves as both an acid and a base / reacts with both acids and bases.

hints: Recall the Period 3 sequence $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ basic to $\text{SO}_2$ acidic, which oxide in the middle near the metal to non-metal border shows both characters.
walkthrough:
Locate the borderline oxide**
Across Period 3, oxides change from basic ($\text{Na}_2\text{O}$, $\text{MgO}$) through amphoteric to acidic ($\text{SiO}_2$, $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$, $\text{SO}_2$). Aluminium sits on the metal to metalloid border, so $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ is the classic amphoteric Period 3 oxide.

hints: Sort the oxides by melting point and structure type, very low values suggest simple molecules while very high values suggest giant ionic or giant covalent lattices.
Distinguish the two simple molecular oxides, bent polar $\text{SO}_2$ with only dipole attractions versus $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ which can hydrogen bond.
Distinguish the three giant structures, $\text{SiO}_2$ must break strong covalent bonds while $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{MgO}$ must break ionic bonds.
walkthrough:
Identify the simple molecular oxides**
$\text{SO}_2$ melts at $-73^{\circ}\text{C}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ at $0^{\circ}\text{C}$. These low values tell you no strong covalent or ionic lattice is broken, only weak intermolecular forces between small molecules. $\text{SO}_2$ is polar but cannot hydrogen bond, so the strongest force broken is permanent dipole to permanent dipole, p.d. $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ has $\text{H}$ bonded to $\text{O}$, so it hydrogen bonds, H, giving it the higher of the two melting points.

Identify the giant covalent oxide**
$\text{SiO}_2$ melts at $1610^{\circ}\text{C}$. This very high value with a non-metal oxide signals a giant covalent network. Melting requires breaking strong $\text{Si-O}$ covalent bonds, so C.

Identify the giant ionic oxides**
$\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ ($1132^{\circ}\text{C}$) and $\text{MgO}$ ($2852^{\circ}\text{C}$) are metal oxides with high melting points characteristic of giant ionic lattices. Melting breaks ionic bonds, so I for both. $\text{MgO}$ is higher because $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ has higher charge and smaller size than $\text{Na}^{+}$, but the force type is still ionic.

Final answer: $\text{SO}_2$ (-73): p.d. ; $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (0): H
$\text{SiO}_2$ (1610): C
$\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ (1132): I and $\text{MgO}$ (2852): I

hints: Ask yourself what actually breaks when $\text{SO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ melt, is it the $\text{S=O}$ or $\text{O-H}$ covalent bonds inside the molecule.
Check whether the table gives you any data about the strength of the $\text{S=O}$ or $\text{O-H}$ covalent bonds themselves, or only about the forces between molecules.
walkthrough:
Test what melting actually measures**
The hypothesis is about the strength of covalent bonds between atoms inside non-metal oxide molecules. But your table shows $\text{SO}_2$ breaks p.d. forces and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ breaks hydrogen bonds on melting. The $\text{S=O}$ and $\text{O-H}$ covalent bonds stay intact, molecules just move apart.

Conclude why data is insufficient**
Only $\text{SiO}_2$ actually breaks covalent bonds on melting, so you have just one example where melting point reflects covalent strength. With no data on the real $\text{S-O}$ or $\text{O-H}$ bond energies, you cannot compare covalent strength with melting point. Hence there is not enough information to say if the hypothesis is true or false.

Final answer: Not enough information to conclude.
Melting of $\text{SO}_2$ and / or $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ breaks intermolecular forces, not covalent bonds / only $\text{SiO}_2$ breaks covalent bonds on melting.
